title: Post-herpetic neuralgia: currently available oral and topical medications in the management of pain – a review
journal: Journal of Pre-Clinical and Clinical Research
article_subtype: Review of oral and topical medications for post-herpetic neuralgia pain
condition_or_topic: Pain management in post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) using oral and topical medications
clinical_background: PHN is a chronic neuropathic pain condition that persists for at least three months after herpes zoster and can substantially impair quality of life. It is the most common chronic complication of herpes zoster, with risk increasing with age; it develops in about 20% of affected patients over the age of 65 and as many as 30% over the age of 80. Older and immunocompromised people are particularly affected. Pain control remains difficult despite the availability of multiple medications, and adverse effects are an important consideration, especially in older patients with other illnesses or concurrent medications.
objectives: Summarize current literature on oral and topical medications available for neuropathic pain associated with PHN, with particular attention to their effectiveness and safety.
study_design: Review of 49 scientific publications published between 2008–2024 and identified through PubMed, PubMedCentral, NCBI and Via Medica Journals. The review examines the effectiveness and safety of oral and topical medications for neuropathic pain in PHN.
interpretation: Pain control in post-herpetic neuralgia remains difficult despite the availability of oral and topical medicines. The authors consider gabapentinoids and tricyclic antidepressants the principal oral first-line options, while emphasizing that treatment should be tailored to the patient and may require medicines with different mechanisms of action. The place of lidocaine 5% patches remains uncertain because efficacy findings and guideline positions conflict. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are generally positioned as second-line options, although opioids are sometimes placed in the third line because of their risks and limited efficacy for neuropathic pain.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The review reports that an analysis of 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for pain relief in post-herpetic neuralgia, but associated with more frequent adverse effects. A meta-analysis of four randomized trials involving 1,272 patients found a single application of an 8% capsaicin patch significantly more effective than 0.014% topical capsaicin. Evidence for lidocaine 5% patches is inconsistent: some studies reported significant pain reduction versus placebo, whereas a double-blind trial found no significant difference. In one study, gabapentin combined with morphine controlled pain more effectively than either drug alone, but adverse events were frequent. These findings are evidence discussed by the authors, not results of new trials conducted in this review.
clinical_implications: Because post-herpetic neuralgia commonly affects older people with other illnesses and concomitant medicines, adverse effects and altered drug handling can complicate pain treatment.
Using medicines with different mechanisms may improve analgesia when one medicine is inadequate, potentially allowing lower doses, provided the combination is safe for the patient.

The low systemic absorption of topical lidocaine and capsaicin limits systemic exposure, although local reactions remain relevant; the authors also describe a low risk of interactions when gabapentinoids are combined with topical medicines.
Renal failure, particularly in patients receiving dialysis, increases concern about gabapentinoid toxicity. Respiratory depression has been described with combined gabapentinoid and opioid use.
practice_implications: Individualize medicine selection according to the clinical case, including comorbidities, concomitant medicines and susceptibility to adverse effects.
Consider gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants as oral first-line treatment, either alone or, when appropriate, alongside topical lidocaine 5% or capsaicin 8%.

Consider multimodal treatment with medicines acting through different mechanisms when monotherapy does not provide adequate analgesia or adverse effects prevent an effective dose, as long as the regimen is safe for the patient.

Use caution with tricyclic antidepressants in patients with cardiac disease and in older patients; the authors suggest considering desipramine or nortriptyline in older patients because of their more linear pharmacokinetics and lower cholinolytic activity than amitriptyline.
Exercise particular care with gabapentinoids in renal failure and when they are combined with opioids, especially in older patients.
Reserve opioids for second- or, in some circumstances, third-line treatment or for multimodal therapy. The authors state that they should not be used in patients with respiratory failure.
Include psychological and social support in a multidisciplinary approach to this chronic condition.
limitations: The authors identify a lack of current guidelines specifically focused on post-herpetic neuralgia and a shortage of long-term studies with sufficiently large patient groups.
Evidence concerning desipramine and nortriptyline is inconclusive; the authors note that relevant studies have often enrolled too few patients and lasted too little time to provide high-quality data.
Studies of lidocaine 5% patches have reached conflicting conclusions about efficacy. The retrospective review reporting a reduction in pain and its affected area included only eight patients.
open_questions: The efficacy and risks of individual medicines and combinations in specific groups of patients with post-herpetic neuralgia remain to be established.
The appropriate first- or second-line position of lidocaine 5% patches remains unresolved because studies and guidelines disagree about their efficacy.
Larger, more thorough studies are needed to confirm the reported analgesic effects of ketamine and assess adverse effects during chronic use.
future_directions: Study the efficacy and risks of specific medicines and combinations in defined patient groups to support more individualized treatment.
Investigate ketamine in larger patient groups, including its safety with chronic use.

Continue evaluating Olodanrigan (EMA401), while accounting for hepatotoxicity detected in preclinical studies during long-term use; the authors note that this toxicity was not observed in the phase II study that ended prematurely.
Continue research on LX9211, described as being in Phase II clinical trials, and LAT8881 as potential future treatments.

tables.summary: The table groups gabapentinoids and tricyclic antidepressants under first-line treatment, and opioids and topical agents under second-line treatment. It identifies neurological, gastrointestinal and other systemic adverse effects for oral drugs, while the listed effects of topical agents chiefly involve the application site.

main_conclusion: Adequate pain relief in post-herpetic neuralgia remains difficult despite the available oral and topical treatments. The authors favor individualized selection of gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants, alone or with topical 5% lidocaine or 8% capsaicin, and call for further research on treatment efficacy and risks in specific patient groups.
narrative_summary:
This review examined the efficacy and safety of oral and topical medications for post-herpetic neuralgia using 49 scientific publications published between 2008–2024. The condition is a persistent neuropathic pain complication of herpes zoster that particularly affects older adults, in whom comorbidities and concurrent medications complicate treatment. Even the most effective approaches achieve a pain-intensity reduction of at least 50% in less than half of patients.

The authors identify gabapentinoids and tricyclic antidepressants as first-line oral options. A review of 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for pain relief, but associated with more frequent adverse effects. Dizziness and somnolence are important gabapentinoid effects; tricyclic antidepressants can produce anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects. Opioids are generally second-line, sometimes third-line, because of limited efficacy in neuropathic pain and risks including dependence and respiratory depression.

The position of 5% lidocaine patches varies across guidelines because efficacy findings conflict, although systemic adverse effects are rare. Capsaicin 8% patches are considered second-line; a meta-analysis of four randomized trials involving 1,272 patients found one application significantly more effective than 0.014% topical capsaicin. When one medication provides insufficient relief or dose-limiting adverse effects occur, the authors describe combinations of agents with different mechanisms as an option. They emphasize tailoring treatment to the patient and investigating the benefits and risks of specific regimens further.

main_findings.description: Studies cited in the review found immediate-release gabapentin more effective than placebo for PHN symptoms.

main_findings.context: The review also describes these extended-release formulations as easier to dose and more bioavailable.

main_findings.context: The study lasted 11-week and evaluated 1,800mg per day.

main_findings.description: Across randomized clinical trials cited in the review, pregabalin relieved PHN pain more effectively than gabapentin, but adverse effects occurred more frequently with pregabalin.
main_findings.context: The comparison was based on 14 randomized clinical trials.

main_findings.description: A cited meta-analysis of placebo-controlled TCAs studies, primarily involving amitriptyline, found benefit for neuropathic pain.
main_findings.context: The outcome concerns neuropathic pain; the review does not present it as an estimate specific to PHN.

main_findings.description: The review finds the evidence for desipramine and nortriptyline in neuropathic pain inconclusive because the cited clinical trials and meta-analyses reach conflicting conclusions.
main_findings.context: The review notes that studies often enrolled too few patients and ran for too short a period to provide high-quality evidence.

main_findings.description: A cited study found transdermal oxycodone effective in patients with severe paresthesia and associated it with fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects than oral oxycodone.
main_findings.context: The review presents this as evidence for particular patients, not for all patients with PHN.

main_findings.description: Studies cited on topical lidocaine patches reached conflicting conclusions: some found significant pain reduction against placebo, whereas a double-blind placebo-controlled trial found no significant difference in pain control.
main_findings.context: The trial reporting no significant difference compared a 5% lidocaine patch with placebo and considered patch treatment relatively safe.

main_findings.description: A cited retrospective review reported less pain and a smaller painful area after topical lidocaine treatment.
main_findings.context: The review included eight patients; the reduction was observed after three months of therapy.

main_findings.description: A cited meta-analysis found a single application of an 8% capsaicin patch significantly more effective for PHN neuropathic pain than 0.014% topical capsaicin.
main_findings.context: The meta-analysis comprised four randomized trials involving 1,272 PHN patients.

main_findings.description: A cited observational study reported short- and medium-term relief of peripheral neuropathic pain with 8% capsaicin patches, alongside a reduction in the painful area.
main_findings.context: The review identifies the studied condition as peripheral neuropathic pain rather than limiting this finding to PHN.

main_findings.description: In a cited study, combined gabapentin and morphine controlled PHN neuropathic pain more effectively than either medication alone, but the combination also had a high incidence of adverse events.
main_findings.context: Reported events with the combination included sedation, constipation, dry mouth, nausea and vomiting.

main_findings.description: The review cites evidence that combined pregabalin and lidocaine 5% was effective for PHN when other single-medication options had not provided adequate pain relief.

Several small studies cited in the review reported neuropathic pain relief with Ketamine, but the review states that larger and more thorough studies are needed to confirm efficacy and assess risks during chronic use.
main_findings.context: These findings concern neuropathic pain and are not presented as definitive evidence for PHN.

main_findings.description: Two cited phase II trials in PHN patients yielded promising findings and a favourable safety profile for Olodanrigan (EMA401).
main_findings.context: One trial ended early because long-term preclinical studies detected hepatotoxicity; that toxicity was not observed in the trial itself.

notable_adverse_events: Gabapentin: dizziness occurred in 19% of patients taking it.
Gabapentin: drowsiness occurred in 14% of patients taking it; balance disorders were also reported.
Pregabalin: dizziness occurred in 24% of patients taking it.
Pregabalin: drowsiness occurred in 17% of patients taking it.

Pregabalin: moderate weight gain may affect up to 25% of patients taking it; in most patients treated with pregabalin, weight gain within a year of starting therapy does not exceed 7% of baseline weight.
Gabapentinoids: gastrointestinal adverse effects described as relatively common include bloating, constipation, appetite disturbance and nausea.

Gabapentin withdrawal: cited case reports place symptom onset between 12 hours and seven days after the last dose. Commonly reported symptoms were agitation, confusion, tremor, insomnia, gastric symptoms and excessive sweating; isolated reports described akathisia, catatonia and convulsions.
Gabapentinoids: toxicity in renal failure, particularly among dialysis patients, may manifest as sedation, confusion, imbalance, tremors, myoclonus or ataxia.
Gabapentinoids combined with opioids: cases of respiratory depression have been described.
TCAs: reported effects include visual disturbances, dry mouth, tachycardia and constipation.
TCAs: reported effects include orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.
TCAs: increased appetite and weight gain may occur.
TCAs: arrhythmias and QTc prolongation are risks relevant to patients with cardiac disease.
Opioids: chronic use carries a high risk of psychological and physical dependence.

Opioids: constipation is very common and may occur after a single dose; nausea is also common. Constipation may prompt dose reduction or discontinuation and thereby leave pain inadequately controlled.

Opioids: other very common reported adverse effects include dizziness, vomiting, myoclonus and muscle rigidity. The review links dizziness in older patients to a greater risk of falls and serious fractures.
Opioids: respiratory-centre depression is reported, and the review states that these medications should not be used in patients with respiratory failure.
Lidocaine 5% patches: reactions at the application site mainly include redness, swelling and itching.

Lidocaine patches: systemic reactions are described as extremely rare and include dizziness, a metallic taste, drowsiness, hypotension and bradycardia; respiratory and cardiac disturbances are described as possible in extreme cases.
Capsaicin 8% patches: local burning pain, pruritus and erythema may lead some patients to discontinue treatment.
Capsaicin 8% patches: a temporary rise in blood pressure may occur; systemic effects are described as very unlikely because skin application results in minimal bloodstream absorption.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most frequent chronic complication of herpes zoster. It is a form of neuropathic pain that can substantially impair quality of life, particularly in older or immunocompromised people, despite the availability of vaccination. This review examines the effectiveness and safety of oral and topical medicines for PHN-related neuropathic pain. It draws on 49 scientific publications identified through PubMed, PubMedCentral, NCBI and Via Medica Journals and published between 2008–2024. Pharmacological treatment includes several oral and topical drug groups. Gabapentinoids and tricyclic anti-depressants are regarded as first-line options; lidocaine 5% patches have that position in some circumstances. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are considered second-line options. Because monotherapy relatively often fails to control pain, multimodal treatment is increasingly used. PHN remains difficult to manage, and the review emphasizes combining medicines with different mechanisms of action and selecting treatment according to the individual clinical situation.

document_sections.heading: Definition and epidemiology.
document_sections.content: PHN is unilateral chronic neuropathic pain in affected dermatomes that continues for at least three months after herpes zoster (HZ) develops. The pain is usually burning, stabbing or throbbing. It is the most common HZ complication, and its likelihood rises with age. Estimates indicate that PHN develops after HZ in about 20% of patients over the age of 65 and as many as 30% over the age of 80. Older adults, immunocompromised people, people with chronic diseases and pregnant women are identified as groups at particular risk following HZ.

document_sections.heading: Pathogenesis of postherpetic neuralgia.
document_sections.content: Impaired host immune defenses permit reactivation of varicella zoster virus. Viral replication in spinal dorsal root ganglia increases pro-inflammatory cytokines. The ensuing inflammation produces a strong local sympathetic response, with vasoconstriction, nerve ischaemia and progressive injury that generate pain involving peripheral and central nerves. Changes arising during acute HZ can disrupt nervous-system function. Over time, descending central pain inhibition may diminish, sensory regions may enlarge, and activity of genes involved in neuropeptide synthesis may change. These processes contribute to the peripheral and central sensitization characteristic of PHN, including spontaneous firing of hyperactive neurons in the spinal dorsal horn. Manifestations include continuous or intermittent spontaneous pain described as burning, throbbing or electric shock-like; allodynia, or pain provoked by a normally nonpainful stimulus; hyperalgesia, or an excessive pain response to a stimulus; paresthesias; and dysesthesias.

document_sections.heading: Available oral and topical medications for pain management in PHN.
document_sections.content: PHN-related neuropathic pain remains difficult to control. Treatment selection must account for the greater risk of adverse effects in older people, who commonly have multiple medicines, chronic illnesses and age-related metabolic changes affecting drug pharmacokinetics. No single treatment is a gold standard: even the most effective approaches achieve a reduction in pain intensity of at least 50% in less than half of patients. Treatment decisions are also hampered by the absence of current PHN-specific guidelines and sufficiently large, long-term studies. The 2004 American Academy of Neurology (AAN) guidelines are considered outdated, have been withdrawn and are no longer supported by the AAN. If safe for the patient, treatment with at least two medicines acting through different mechanisms appears to offer the best prospect of effective pain control. Because PHN is chronic and often impairs daily life, multidisciplinary care should include psychological and social support. Neuropathic-pain guidelines consistently place tricyclic anti-depressants (TCAs) and gabapentinoids first-line. Although 5% lidocaine patches were previously widely recommended first-line for PHN, disagreement among current guidelines and conflicting study findings leave their first- versus second-line position uncertain. Capsaicin 8% patches or cream and opioids are placed second-line.

document_sections.heading: Gabapentinoids.
document_sections.content: Gabapentin and pregabalin were initially used for epilepsy and are now recommended first-line for PHN and other neuropathic pain. Although structurally related to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), they do not bind its receptors; they attach to the α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Proposed analgesic mechanisms include limiting excessive, α2δ-1-dependent release of neurotransmitters involved in pain transmission, reducing α2δ-1 accumulation in synaptic vesicles of spinal dorsal root ganglia, and activating descending noradrenergic inhibition. Neither drug binds plasma proteins or undergoes metabolism by liver enzymes, and they do not alter concentrations of drugs metabolized by cytochrome CYP450. Both are eliminated chiefly in urine. Depending on dose, gabapentin has a half-life of five to seven hours; pregabalin has a half-life of about 6.3 hours. Oral gabapentin is supplied in immediate-release and extended-release forms. Studies found immediate-release gabapentin more effective than placebo for PHN symptoms at 1,800mg to 3,600mg per day. Its non-linear gastrointestinal absorption lowers bioavailability as doses rise, complicating titration to an effective dose without adverse reactions. A Cochrane Review found the extended-release formulations gastroretentive gabapentin and gabapentin enacarbil more effective than placebo for PHN; these formulations are easier to dose and have greater bioavailability. Gastroretentive gabapentin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract for up to 15h and is taken once daily. Its recommended starting dose is 900mg per day, followed by gradual titration to a therapeutic dose over two weeks. An 11-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase three study demonstrated PHN pain control with 1,800mg per day. Gabapentin enacarbil is a prodrug that needs less frequent administration than immediate-release gabapentin and produces less variation in plasma concentration. Its minimum therapeutic dose is 1,200mg per day, reached through gradual dosing over four days. Compared with gabapentin, pregabalin has high bioavailability and linear gastrointestinal absorption, making its pharmacokinetics more predictable; maximum plasma concentration follows oral dosing after one hour. An assessment based on 14 randomized clinical trials found pregabalin more effective than gabapentin for PHN pain but associated with more frequent side-effects. Its recommended starting dose is 150mg/day in two or three divided doses, with gradual titration over about one week; the maximum recommended, relatively well-tolerated therapeutic dose is 600mg/day. Common central nervous system effects include dizziness, reported in 19% when taking gabapentin, and balance disorders and drowsiness, with drowsiness reported at 14% for gabapetin. With pregabalin, dizziness occurred in 24% and drowsiness in 17%. Moderate weight gain can occur with gabapentinoids and may affect up to 25% of pregabalin users, although for most patients receiving pregabalin the gain within a year does not exceed 7% of baseline weight. Bloating, constipation, altered appetite and nausea are relatively common. Gabapentinoids may also produce withdrawal symptoms. In available case reports, symptoms after stopping gabapentin began between 12 hours and seven days after the last dose; agitation, confusion, tremor, insomnia, gastric symptoms and excessive sweating were most frequent, while akathisia, catatonia and convulsions were reported in isolated cases. Renal failure raises the risk of gabapentinoid toxicity, particularly in dialysis patients, because these drugs are excreted in urine. Toxicity may present with sedation, confusion, impaired balance, tremors, myoclonus or ataxia. Respiratory depression has been described with combined gabapentinoid and opioid administration. Particular care is therefore required in older people, among whom respiratory disease and opioid use are common.

document_sections.heading: Tricyclic ant-idepressants.
document_sections.content: Tricyclic anti-depressants (TCAs), originally developed for depression, are widely used off-label as first-line treatment for PHN pain in the United States and elsewhere despite lacking Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for that purpose. They inhibit re-uptake of norepinephrine and serotonin from the post-synaptic gap, probably stimulating descending noradrenergic and serotonergic pain-inhibitory pathways. Effects on alpha-adrenergic receptors and sodium-channel blockade may also modify neuropathic pain. Amitriptyline is the best-studied member of the group and can affect neuropathic pain at doses below those needed for an antidepressant effect. A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled TCA studies, mainly involving amitriptyline, found benefit for neuropathic pain, with a Number Needed to Treat of 3.6. Findings on desipramine and nortriptyline are inconclusive because trials and meta-analyses conflict; studies have often enrolled too few patients and been too short to provide high-quality evidence. For PHN, TCAs should be started at 10–25mg/day and, according to individual tolerability, may be gradually increased to 75–100mg/day. They are metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes and have half-lives ranging from 10 – 28 hours. Their multiple receptor actions can cause visual disturbance, dry mouth, tachycardia and constipation through muscarinic effects; orthostatic hypotension or dizziness through alpha-adrenergic blockade; and increased appetite or weight through histamine-receptor interactions. Cardiac patients require caution because TCAs may cause arrhythmias and prolong the QTc interval. Older patients are especially susceptible to adverse effects owing to polypharmacy, age-related metabolic changes and greater sensitivity to cholinolytic effects. Desipramine or nortriptyline may be considered in this population because their pharmacokinetics are more linear and their cholinolytic activity is lower than that of amitriptyline.

document_sections.heading: Opioids.
document_sections.content: Morphine was the first opioid used to treat pain and was isolated from opium in the early 19th century. Other opioids subsequently developed include tramadol, buprenorphine and oxycodone. Their antinociceptive action involves opioid receptors in the brain, spinal cord and peripheral tissues, chiefly MOP, for which most exogenous opioids have the greatest affinity; the other main receptor types are KOP and DOP. Receptor stimulation inhibits transmission of painful stimuli. Opioid effectiveness is reduced in neuropathic pain. Possible mechanisms include reduced MOP receptor-protein expression in the spinal dorsal horn and increased activity of pain-transmitting neuropeptides such as substance P after nerve injury. Because of limited efficacy for neuropathic pain and associated risks, opioids are currently regarded as second-line and sometimes only third-line therapy. They may be combined with other medicines or used for PHN pain while TCAs or gabapentinoids are titrated to their intended therapeutic effect. Administration for PHN is mainly oral, although studies and case reports suggest that transdermal delivery can control pain in selected patients. In one study involving people with severe paresthesia, transdermal oxycodone was effective and caused fewer gastrointestinal side-effects than oral oxycodone. Transdermal opioids may sometimes work better for patients who have difficulty following dosing instructions or taking oral medication. Prolonged opioid treatment carries potentially serious consequences, including substantial risks of physical and psychological dependence. Common adverse effects include constipation and nausea; constipation can occur after a single dose and may prompt dose reduction or discontinuation, leaving pain inadequately treated. Other very common effects are dizziness, which increases falls and serious fracture risk particularly in older people, vomiting, myoclonus and muscle rigidity. Opioids also suppress the brainstem respiratory centre and should not be used in patients with respiratory failure. These adverse effects and dependence risks support their use as second- or third-line PHN treatment or within multimodal therapy.

document_sections.heading: Topical drugs.
document_sections.content: Lidocaine and capsaicin are used topically for PHN-related neuropathic pain. The Lidocaine 5% patch is FDA-approved for PHN in the United States. In Europe, it is recommended first-line, particularly for non-severe pain affecting a limited area and as part of combination treatment. Lidocaine stabilizes neuronal membrane potential by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels and suppresses ectopic activity in injured nerves. Studies of topical lidocaine have reached conflicting conclusions for PHN and other neuropathic pain: some report significantly less pain than with placebo. A retrospective review of only eight patients reported reduced pain and an average 66% reduction in the painful area after three months of treatment. Conversely, a double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial found no significant difference in pain control between the 5% lidocaine patch and placebo, while noting its comparatively low adverse-effect risk. The 2020 S2k guidelines for herpes zoster and PHN diagnosis and treatment recommend treating 5% lidocaine as a second-choice PHN medicine. Limited bloodstream absorption from the patch contributes to its relative safety. Adverse effects are predominantly application-site redness, swelling or itching. Systemic reactions are extremely rare but may include dizziness, a metallic taste, drowsiness, hypotension and bradycardia, or, in extreme cases, respiratory and cardiac disturbances. Capsaicin 8% patches are considered second-line for PHN, are FDA-approved for this indication and can form part of combination therapy. Capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors, prompting release of vasoactive neuropeptides, particularly substance P, followed by calcium influx that disrupts neuronal mitochondria. The resulting dysfunction of nerve endings prevents nociceptive stimulation in the treated area. This effect can persist from several weeks to as long as three months, and a single patch contains enough capsaicin to produce the intended analgesia. A meta-analysis of four randomized trials involving 1,272 PHN patients found one application of an 8% capsaicin patch significantly more effective against neuropathic pain than 0.014% topical capsaicin. An observational study reported short- and medium-term benefit from 8% capsaicin patches for peripheral neuropathic pain, along with a smaller painful area. Although generally well tolerated, the 8% patch may cause local burning pain, pruritus and erythema that lead some patients to stop treatment; transient blood-pressure elevation is also possible. Minimal absorption through the skin makes systemic effects very unlikely.

document_sections.heading: Combination therapy.
document_sections.content: For PHN, combination treatment may be appropriate when monotherapy provides insufficient analgesia or adverse effects prevent an effective TCA or gabapentinoid dose. Several studies describe advantages of combining oral and topical medicines over monotherapy. Different mechanisms of action may permit the desired effect with lower doses of two drug groups while limiting adverse effects. In one study, gabapentin plus morphine controlled PHN-related neuropathic pain better than either medicine alone, but adverse events were frequent, including sedation, constipation, dry mouth, nausea and vomiting. Combining gabapentinoids with topical medicines is of particular interest because the risk of drug interactions is low. Pregabalin with lidocaine 5% has provided effective treatment for people with PHN whose other single-drug options gave insufficient relief.

document_sections.heading: Future directions in the treatment of post-herpetic neuralgia.
document_sections.content: Even with medicines acting through different mechanisms, PHN-related neuropathic pain can remain difficult to treat, sometimes without satisfactory relief. New pharmaceuticals are under investigation. Ketamine relieved neuropathic pain in several studies with small patient groups, but larger, more detailed studies are needed to verify those findings and assess adverse effects during chronic use. Type 2 receptor antagonists for Angiotensin II may have potential for neuropathic pain syndromes including PHN. Olodanrigan (EMA401), a highly selective antagonist of that receptor, produced promising findings and a good safety profile in PHN patients in two phase II trials. One of those studies ended early because long-term preclinical studies detected hepatotoxicity with Olodanrigan; hepatotoxicity was not observed in the trial itself. Other agents under investigation are the adaptor-related kinase 1 inhibitor LX9211, currently in Phase II clinical trials, and LAT8881, a human growth-hormone fragment whose action depends on the peptide-modifying enzymes LANCL1 and LANCL2.

document_sections.heading: SUMMARY
document_sections.content: Adequate control of PHN pain remains difficult despite the available oral and topical medicines. Because PHN commonly affects older people with additional diseases and existing medications, clinicians need to understand treatment mechanisms and possible adverse effects. The review considers oral gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants the most appropriate current first-line options, either alone or combined with topical 5% lidocaine or 8% capsaicin. Further research is needed to establish the efficacy and risks of individual medicines and combinations in specific PHN patient groups, enabling more individualized treatment. Continued research and clinical trials of new drugs may yield additional safe and effective options.
